title: Music Production
summary: Learn to make music from idea to release: rhythm, tempo and harmony for producers, setting up a home studio and DAW, making beats and arranging, recording vocals and instruments, mixing and mastering, and releasing music, copyright and royalties. Calculations were checked in code.
audience: Aspiring producers, beatmakers, artists and anyone who wants to make music at home

body.p: Music production is the process of creating, recording, arranging, mixing and finishing music. Today a laptop or even a phone can be a full studio, which has helped producers across Africa create genres heard worldwide, such as Afrobeats, amapiano, bongo flava and gqom.

Tempo is measured in beats per minute (BPM). At 120 BPM each beat lasts 60 / 120 = 0.5 seconds, so a bar of four beats lasts 2 seconds and 16 bars last 32 seconds. Many amapiano tracks sit around 110 to 115 BPM; much Afrobeats sits around 100 to 115 BPM. At 100 BPM, an 8-bar section in 4/4 lasts 60 / 100 x 4 x 8 = 19.2 seconds.

list: Notes are arranged in scales; the major scale sounds bright, the minor scale often darker or more emotional.
Chords are three or more notes played together; chord progressions give songs their emotional journey.
Bass lines connect rhythm and harmony and are central to many African dance styles.
Learning a little keyboard makes programming melodies and chords much faster.

body.tip: Study songs you love: count the BPM, note when each instrument enters and how sections are arranged.

body.p: A digital audio workstation (DAW) is software for recording, arranging and mixing. Options include FL Studio (widely used for Afrobeats and amapiano), Ableton Live, Logic Pro, Reaper (low cost), Cakewalk and free mobile apps.

list: A computer with enough memory, and an audio interface to connect microphones and speakers with low delay.
Studio headphones and, if possible, monitor speakers with a flat, honest sound.
A MIDI keyboard to play notes into the DAW.
A microphone: a large-diaphragm condenser is common for vocals; a dynamic microphone handles noisy rooms better.

body.p: CD-quality audio uses a sample rate of 44 100 samples per second at 16-bit depth. For stereo, that is 44 100 x 16 x 2 = 1411.2 kilobits per second, so a 3-minute track is about 31.8 MB uncompressed. Compressed formats such as MP3 and AAC are much smaller.

body.tip: Treat your room before buying expensive gear: blankets, curtains, foam or bookshelves reduce echo and improve recordings.

list: Drums: kick, snare or clap, hi-hats and percussion such as shakers, congas and log drums form the groove.
Programming: use the piano roll or step sequencer; vary velocity (how hard notes hit) and add swing so the groove feels human.
Bass: lock it with the kick drum; in amapiano the log drum bass is a signature sound.
Chords and melody: pads, keys, guitars and synths.
Samples: short recordings of sounds or music. Clear samples from other people's records before releasing, or use royalty-free sample packs.

body.p: Arrangement is how a song develops over time. A common pop structure is intro, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, verse, chorus, bridge, final chorus and outro. Dance tracks often build and release energy over 8- and 16-bar sections. Adding or removing elements, such as dropping the drums before the chorus, keeps listeners engaged.

body.tip: Make a full rough version of a song before perfecting any one part; many producers get stuck polishing an endless 8-bar loop.

steps: Prepare: warm up the singer, print lyrics and set a comfortable headphone mix.
Position the microphone about a hand's width to 20 cm from the singer, with a pop filter to stop plosive bursts from P and B sounds.
Set the input level so loud parts peak around -10 to -6 dB, leaving headroom and never clipping.
Record several takes and keep notes of the best lines.
Comp the vocal: combine the best parts of different takes into one performance.

body.p: Emotion matters more than technical perfection. Make artists comfortable, encourage them, and record in short sections when needed. Record backing vocals, ad-libs and harmonies to add depth.
Recording live instruments, such as guitar, saxophone, talking drum or mbira, gives tracks character that programmed sounds cannot fully match.

body.tip: Record at 24-bit to capture more detail and allow more headroom than 16-bit.

body.p: Mixing balances all the elements so the song sounds clear and powerful on any system.

list: Levels: set volume balance first; most problems are solved by good levels.
Panning: place sounds left, centre or right to create width; keep kick, bass and lead vocal in the centre.
EQ (equalisation): cut or boost frequencies, for example removing low rumble from vocals and making room for the kick and bass.
Compression: controls dynamics, making quiet and loud parts more even and adding punch.
Reverb and delay: create space and depth; use them carefully to avoid a muddy mix.

body.p: Loudness is measured in decibels, a logarithmic scale. Doubling power adds about 3 dB (10 log₁₀ 2 = 3.01), and doubling amplitude adds about 6 dB. Our ears are easily fooled by louder sounds, so compare changes at matched volume.

Mastering is the final step that makes a track sound consistent and competitive across streaming platforms, adjusting overall EQ, compression and loudness. Streaming services normalise loudness, so crushing a master to make it as loud as possible usually just removes dynamics.

body.tip: Check mixes on phone speakers, earphones and a car stereo; most listeners will hear your music on these.

list: Distribution: digital distributors place music on streaming platforms such as Spotify, Apple Music, Audiomack and Boomplay.
Metadata: correct song titles, artist names, songwriters and ISRC codes ensure you are paid.

Copyright: you own the copyright in your original music and recordings; register works with your country's collecting society (such as SAMRO in South Africa, MCSK in Kenya or COSON in Nigeria) to collect royalties.
Split sheets: agree in writing who wrote what percentage of a song before release to avoid disputes.
Contracts: read and understand producer, management and label agreements; get advice before signing.

body.p: Producers earn from beat sales and leases, production fees, royalties and publishing, sync licensing for adverts and films, live performances and teaching. Building a brand, collaborating, and releasing consistently matter as much as technical skill.

body.tip: Back up project files and stems; artists and labels often ask for them years later.
